mainTopic: רבי חייא's rebuke of רב, אביי's rulings on the status of a person's hand on שבת, and the ways the גמרא reconciles two ברייתות about bringing back a hand stretched outside
overview: Earlier, רב asked רבי about someone who was loaded with food and drink and then walked out on שבת. רבי answered: 'חייב, and it is not like his hand.' Here רבי חייא scolds רב for asking רבי about a different מסכתא while רבי was busy with another one. He then admits the answer was correct and proves it from a ברייתא. Next, אביי says it is obvious that a person's hand is neither רשות הרבים nor רשות היחיד. He proves this from the משנה's cases of the poor man and the homeowner. אביי then asks whether the hand counts as a כרמלית, meaning whether the חכמים forbade bringing it back. The גמרא tries to answer from two ברייתות that disagree about bringing back a hand full of fruit. It then explains those ברייתות in several other ways: below or above ten טפחים, before שבת or after dark, by mistake or on purpose, and an argument over קנסו שוגג אטו מזיד. Along the way, the timing answer also settles רב ביבי בר אביי's question about bread stuck in an oven. The amud ends partway through one more explanation, about bringing the hand back to the same חצר, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי חייא scolds רב for asking רבי an off-topic question
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא tells רב that he should not ask רבי about a different מסכתא while רבי is focused on another one. If רבי were not such a great man, he would have been embarrassed into giving a weak answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא said to רב: 'Son of great people! Didn't I tell you that when רבי is busy with one מסכתא, you should not ask him about a different מסכתא, because it may not be on his mind? If רבי were not such a great man, you would have embarrassed him, because he would have had to give you an answer that is not a real answer.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא, who was רב's uncle, scolds רב for asking רבי a question from outside the topic they were studying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is not the content of רב's question. The problem is the timing: a teacher focused on one מסכתא might not have another topic ready in his mind. רבי חייא warns that this could push even a great teacher into a forced, weak answer, which would embarrass him.

keyTerms.meaning: Son of great people (nobles); a respectful way to address רב even while scolding him
A different tractate
It is not on his mind; he is not focused on it right now
You would have embarrassed him
An answer or resolution given to a question

steps.confusionAlert: רבי חייא is NOT saying that רבי's actual answer was wrong. He is describing the danger: had רבי not been so great, the answer might have been weak. The very next line says that this time the answer was good.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya said to Rav:
phrases.notes: רבי חייא was רב's uncle (his mother's brother).

phrases.english: Son of great people!
phrases.notes: A title of respect, even within a rebuke.

phrases.english: Didn't I tell you,
when Rebbi is occupied with this tractate
do not ask him about another tractate,
because perhaps it is not on his mind.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי לָאו דְּרַבִּי גַּבְרָא רַבָּה הוּא —
phrases.english: For if Rebbi were not a great man —
you would have embarrassed him,

phrases.aramaic: דִּמְשַׁנֵּי לָךְ שִׁינּוּיָא דְּלָאו שִׁינּוּיָא הוּא.
phrases.english: since he would answer you with an answer that is not a real answer.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא לְרַב: בַּר פַּחֲתֵי! לָא אָמֵינָא לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to the exchange on the previous amud, where רב asked רבי about someone loaded with food and drink, and רבי answered 'חייב, and it is not like his hand.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A student should not ask his teacher about a different מסכתא while the teacher is focused on another one, because the teacher may be forced into a weak answer and be embarrassed.

steps.title: A ברייתא proves that רבי's answer was correct
steps.stepSummary: Even so, רבי answered well this time. A ברייתא rules the same way: a person loaded before שבת who walks out after dark is חייב, because his body is not like his hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Even so, this time he answered you well. For a ברייתא teaches: If a person was loaded with food and drink while it was still day, and he carried them outside after dark, he is חייב, because this is not like his hand.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא admits that רבי's answer was correct, and he backs it up by quoting a ברייתא that says exactly the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was whether picking things up before שבת means there is no new act of lifting (עקירה) on שבת. The ברייתא says he is still חייב: his body normally stands at rest, so when he starts walking on שבת, that counts as a new lifting of the items. A hand stretched out in the air is different, because it was never resting in a fixed place.

keyTerms.meaning: Now, in any case; even so, this time
As a ברייתא teaches
Loaded, carrying a burden
While it was still day, before שבת began
After dark, once שבת had begun

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that walking with a load counts as a new act of lifting on שבת, even if the load was picked up before שבת. This makes a person's body different from a stretched-out hand.

phrases.english: Now, in any case, he answered you well.
For it was taught in a Baraita:

phrases.aramaic: הָיָה טָעוּן אוֹכָלִין וּמַשְׁקִין מִבְּעוֹד יוֹם,
phrases.english: If one was loaded with food and drink while it was still day,
and he carried them outside after dark —
he is liable,
because it is not similar to his hand.
phrases.notes: The body rests on the ground, so walking counts as lifting. A hand held in the air does not rest.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא מִיהַת שַׁפִּיר מְשַׁנֵּי לָךְ. דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Softens the rebuke in step 1 by admitting that רבי's answer was correct, and proves it from a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רבי's ruling that a person loaded before שבת who walks out on שבת is חייב, because this is not like his hand.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that rules in exactly the same words: חייב, לפי שאינו דומה לידו.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Someone loaded with items before שבת who walks out with them on שבת is חייב. His body is not like his hand.

steps.title: אביי: a person's hand is neither a public nor a private domain
steps.stepSummary: אביי says it is obvious that a person's hand does not take on the status of רשות הרבים or of רשות היחיד. He proves both halves from the משנה's cases of the poor man's hand and the homeowner's hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: It is obvious to me that a person's hand is neither like רשות הרבים nor like רשות היחיד. We know it is not like רשות הרבים from the case of the poor man's hand. We know it is not like רשות היחיד from the case of the homeowner's hand.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי states a rule he considers obvious: a hand stretched into another domain does not count as part of רשות הרבים or of רשות היחיד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, a homeowner takes an item from a poor man's hand that reached into the house, and the homeowner is not חייב. If that hand counted as רשות הרבים, the homeowner would be חייב for bringing the item in. In the reverse case, a poor man takes from a homeowner's hand that reached outside, and he is not חייב. If that hand counted as רשות היחיד, the poor man would be חייב for taking the item out.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious to me
A person's hand
Public domain
Private domain
Poor man, standing outside in the public domain in the משנה
Homeowner, standing inside his house in the משנה

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up אביי's question in the next step. If a hand is neither public nor private, perhaps it is like the in-between rabbinic domain, כרמלית.

phrases.english: Abaye said: It is obvious to me
that a person's hand
is neither like a public domain
nor like a private domain.
It is not like a public domain —
as we see from the poor man's hand.
phrases.notes: The homeowner who takes from the poor man's hand is not liable.

phrases.english: It is not like a private domain —
as we see from the homeowner's hand.
phrases.notes: The poor man who takes from the homeowner's hand is not liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the story with רב and רבי to a new discussion of the legal status of a person's hand.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person's hand stretched into another domain counts as neither רשות הרבים nor רשות היחיד, as the משנה's cases of the poor man and the homeowner show.

steps.title: אביי asks whether the hand is treated like a כרמלית
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks whether a hand holding an object is treated like a כרמלית. In practical terms: did the חכמים penalize him by forbidding him to bring his hand back to himself?
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי asked: What is the status of a person's hand? Is it treated like a כרמלית? In other words, did the חכמים penalize him by forbidding him to bring it back to himself, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי raises a question he is unsure about: is a hand holding an object, stretched into another domain, treated like the rabbinic in-between domain called כרמלית?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the hand is neither public nor private, אביי wonders whether it should be treated like a כרמלית. The practical difference is whether the חכמים made a penalty forbidding the person to pull his hand, with the object, back into the domain where he is standing. אביי leaves both possibilities open as a question.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked; raised a question he could not settle
An in-between domain set up by the חכמים, neither fully public nor fully private
The חכמים penalized him
To bring it back to himself

steps.confusionAlert: This question does not cancel what אביי said in step 3. He still holds that the hand is neither public nor private. He is now asking whether the חכמים gave it a third, in-between status, and whether that leads to a penalty.

phrases.english: Abaye asked:
A person's hand,
what is the law — is it treated like a karmelit?
Did the Sages penalize him
from bringing it back to himself, or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי אַבָּיֵי: יָדוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם, מַהוּ שֶׁתֵּעָשֶׂה כְּכַרְמְלִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 3. Since the hand is neither public nor private, אביי asks whether it takes the in-between status of כרמלית.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a hand holding an object in another domain has the status of כרמלית, meaning whether the חכמים forbade bringing it back to the person as a penalty.

steps.title: Attempted proof from two conflicting ברייתות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings two ברייתות that argue about bringing a fruit-filled hand back inside. It suggests their argument is exactly אביי's question: is the hand like a כרמלית or not?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A man's hand was full of fruit and he stuck it outside. One ברייתא teaches that he may not bring it back, and another ברייתא teaches that he may bring it back. Aren't they arguing about this exact point? One holds the hand is like a כרמלית, and the other holds it is not like a כרמלית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer אביי's question from Step 4 by pointing to two ברייתות that disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the hand is like a כרמלית, then the חכמים would forbid bringing it back, which matches the ברייתא that says אסור. If the hand is not like a כרמלית, there is nothing to forbid, which matches the ברייתא that says מותר. So it looks like אביי's question is really a dispute between two תנאים.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source to answer a question
One ברייתא teaches... and another teaches (two sources that conflict)
An in-between area, neither fully public nor fully private, where the חכמים forbade carrying
Is it not so that...? (a suggested reading the גמרא will test)
They argue

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If his hand was full of fruit
and he stuck it outside,
phrases.notes: He is standing in the private domain and reaches into the public domain.

phrases.english: one ברייתא teaches: it is forbidden to bring it back,
and another teaches: it is permitted to bring it back.
Is it not about this that they argue?
That one master holds it is like a כרמלית,
and the other master holds it is not like a כרמלית?!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הָיְתָה יָדוֹ מְלֵאָה פֵּירוֹת וְהוֹצִיאָהּ לַחוּץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attempts to resolve the שאלה of Step 4 using a pair of ברייתות
steps.raayaObject: Whether a hand holding an object outside is treated like a כרמלית
steps.raayaSupportSource: Two conflicting ברייתות about returning a fruit-filled hand

steps.title: Everyone agrees it is like a כרמלית; the difference is the height
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Both ברייתות agree the hand is like a כרמלית. One speaks about a hand below ten טפחים, and the other about a hand above ten טפחים.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees the hand is like a כרמלית, and there is no contradiction: here he reached out below ten טפחים, and there he reached out above ten טפחים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof by showing the two ברייתות can agree in principle and still rule differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Below ten טפחים, the hand is inside the airspace of רשות הרבים, so it is treated like a כרמלית and he may not bring it back. Above ten טפחים, it is out of that airspace, so the כרמלית concern does not apply and he may bring it back. Since this reading works, the ברייתות do not prove anything about אביי's question.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
And it is not a contradiction
Here... there (each source refers to a different case)
Below ten טפחים from the ground, inside the airspace of רשות הרבים
Above ten טפחים, out of the airspace of רשות הרבים

phrases.english: No, everyone agrees it is like a כרמלית,
and there is no contradiction:
Here, it was below ten טפחים.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא that says אסור לְהַחֲזִירָהּ.

phrases.english: There, it was above ten טפחים.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא that says מותר לְהַחֲזִירָהּ.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 5 by giving the two ברייתות different cases
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the ברייתות argue about the כרמלית question
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתות can be explained as speaking about different heights, so they are not necessarily arguing in principle

steps.title: Second answer: not like a כרמלית; the difference is the time of day
steps.stepSummary: Another way to reject the proof: both ברייתות speak about a hand below ten טפחים and both hold it is not like a כרמלית. The difference is when he reached out. Before שבת he was not penalized; after dark he was.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say instead: both ברייתות speak about below ten טפחים, and the hand is not like a כרמלית. There is still no contradiction: here he reached out while it was still day, and there he reached out after dark. If he reached out while it was still day, the חכמים did not penalize him. If he reached out after dark, the חכמים penalized him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second, different way to explain the two ברייתות, so the proof again falls away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the reason for forbidding is not the כרמלית status. It is a קנס, a penalty, for having done something wrong on שבת. Someone who reached out before שבת did nothing wrong and is not penalized. Someone who reached out on שבת itself is penalized by not being allowed to bring his hand back.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say instead (introduces an alternative answer)
Both this one and that one
While it was still day, before שבת began
After dark, once שבת had begun
The חכמים penalized him

steps.confusionAlert: In this answer the hand is NOT like a כרמלית, yet he is still sometimes forbidden to bring it back. That is because the ban here is a separate penalty for acting on שבת, not because of the hand's location.

phrases.english: And if you want, say instead:
both ברייתות are about below ten טפחים
and the hand is not like a כרמלית,
and there is no contradiction:
here, he reached out while it was still day,
there, he reached out after dark.
While it was still day, the חכמים did not penalize him,
phrases.notes: So he may bring it back.

phrases.english: after dark, the חכמים penalized him.
phrases.notes: So he may not bring it back.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי לְמַטָּה מֵעֲשָׂרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, independent rejection of the proof in Step 5, in place of Step 6's height-based answer
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the ברייתות argue about the כרמלית question
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The difference can come from a קנס based on timing, so the כרמלית question is not involved at all

steps.title: On the contrary: the reverse makes more sense
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the timing answer. Logic says the penalty should apply during the day, when it is safe, and not at night, when penalizing him could lead to a real חטאת.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary, the reverse makes more sense! While it was still day, if he threw the fruit down he would not become liable for a חטאת, so let the חכמים penalize him. After dark, if he threw it down he would become liable for a חטאת, so the חכמים should not penalize him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the second answer from Step 7 by arguing that its logic is backwards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he cannot bring his hand back, he might give up and drop the fruit into רשות הרבים. If he picked it up before שבת, dropping it is not a Torah violation, so a penalty there is safe. If he picked it up on שבת, dropping it completes a Torah-level act of carrying and brings a חטאת. So the חכמים should not make a rule that pushes him toward that.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary
The reverse is more logical
He throws it down
Liability to bring a sin-offering, meaning a Torah-level violation
Let them penalize him

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a key principle about rabbinic penalties: the חכמים will not make a penalty that is likely to push a person into a Torah-level sin.

phrases.english: On the contrary, the reverse makes more sense!
While it was still day,
where if he throws it down
he does not come to liability for a חטאת,
phrases.notes: The picking up happened on a weekday, so the act of carrying is not complete on שבת.

phrases.english: let the חכמים penalize him.
After dark,
where if he throws it down
he comes through them to liability for a חטאת,
phrases.notes: Both the picking up and the putting down would happen on שבת.

phrases.english: the חכמים should not penalize him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the logic of the time-based answer in Step 7
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 7 that the חכמים penalized him after dark but not during the day
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A penalty that blocks his hand from coming back may lead him to drop the object. That is harmless during the day but a Torah-level חטאת at night, so the penalty belongs during the day, not at night.

steps.title: The timing answer would also answer רב ביבי בר אביי's bread question
steps.stepSummary: Since the גמרא kept the answer that he is penalized at night, even with the risk of a חטאת, this seems to answer רב ביבי בר אביי's question. The answer would be that the חכמים do not permit breaking a rabbinic rule to avoid a Torah sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since we did not answer it that way, we can answer רב ביבי בר אביי's question. He asked: if someone stuck bread to the wall of an oven, did they let him take it off before he becomes liable for a חטאת, or not? Answer: they did not let him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out an unexpected result of keeping the timing answer: it would answer a question by רב ביבי בר אביי that was thought to have no answer. This sets up a possible problem, which the גמרא handles in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the hand case, he is penalized at night even though he might drop the object and do a Torah sin. That suggests the חכמים keep their rabbinic penalty even when it risks a Torah sin. Taking bread off an oven wall is only a rabbinic איסור, so by the same logic it should not be permitted, even though leaving the bread means it will bake and he will be חייב חטאת.

keyTerms.meaning: Stuck dough to the wall of an oven (the usual way bread was baked)
To remove it (the bread) from the oven, which is a rabbinic איסור
Liability to bring a sin-offering, meaning a real Torah sin
Resolve it, i.e., answer the open question

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two איסורים here. Taking the bread out is only a rabbinic איסור. Letting it bake is a Torah איסור that brings a חטאת. The question is whether we may do the small איסור to avoid the big one.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the classic question of whether the חכמים allow breaking their own rule to save a person from a Torah sin.

phrases.english: And since we did not answer it that way,
phrases.notes: We did not flip the timing answer. We kept the version where he is penalized at night.

phrases.english: resolve the question of Rav Bivi bar Abaye.
For Rav Bivi bar Abaye asked:
If he stuck bread onto the oven wall,
phrases.notes: He did it by mistake on שבת.

phrases.english: did they permit him to remove it
before he comes to be liable for a sin-offering,
phrases.notes: That is, before the bread finishes baking.

phrases.english: or did they not permit it?
Resolve that they did not permit it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the fact that the timing answer from Step 7 was kept despite the logical challenge in Step 8, and draws a surprising result from it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The timing answer (penalized at night, not before Shabbat).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the timing answer stands, it answers רב ביבי בר אביי's question, which was supposedly left without an answer. That seems problematic.

steps.title: No problem: let the bread question be answered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says this is not a difficulty. We may indeed answer רב ביבי בר אביי's question this way.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not a problem. Go ahead and answer it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the result. It is fine that the timing answer also answers רב ביבי בר אביי's question, so his question is now answered: they did not permit it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry was that רב ביבי בר אביי's question was known to be open. The גמרא says a question being open until now does not mean it cannot be answered. So the timing answer stands, and so does its result for the bread case.

keyTerms.meaning: This is not a difficulty

phrases.english: This is not difficult, and indeed, resolve it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem raised in Step 9 by simply accepting its result.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Answering רב ביבי בר אביי's open question looked like a weakness in the timing answer.
steps.terutzMaskana: There is no problem. רב ביבי בר אביי's question is answered: they did not permit removing the bread.

steps.title: Another explanation: by mistake versus on purpose
steps.stepSummary: Another way to explain the two ברייתות without answering רב ביבי בר אביי's question. One ברייתא speaks about someone who reached out by mistake, and he is not penalized. The other speaks about someone who reached out on purpose, and he is penalized.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: really, do not answer רב ביבי בר אביי's question, and there is still no contradiction. Here he acted by mistake, and there he acted on purpose. By mistake, the חכמים did not penalize him. On purpose, the חכמים penalized him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new way to explain why one ברייתא lets him bring his hand back and the other does not. The difference is whether he reached out by mistake (שוגג) or on purpose (מזיד).
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explanation drops the timing distinction, so nothing here forces an answer to the bread question. The ברייתא that permits bringing the hand back is about a שוגג, who does not deserve a penalty. The ברייתא that forbids it is about a מזיד, whom the חכמים penalized.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say instead (introduces another answer)
Really, actually
Someone who acted by mistake
Someone who acted on purpose
The חכמים penalized him

phrases.english: And if you want, say: actually, do not resolve it,

here it is by mistake, there it is on purpose.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different way to explain the two ברייתות from Step 5, instead of the timing answer from Step 7, so that רב ביבי בר אביי's question does not have to be answered.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות could only be explained by timing, which forces an answer to the bread question.
steps.terutzMaskana: The permitting ברייתא is about a שוגג, and the forbidding ברייתא is about a מזיד.

steps.title: A third explanation: do we penalize a mistake because of on-purpose cases?
steps.stepSummary: Both ברייתות speak about someone who acted by mistake. They argue whether the חכמים penalize a שוגג so that people do not come to act on purpose.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: both ברייתות are about someone who acted by mistake. They argue whether the חכמים penalized a mistaken person because of a deliberate one. One master holds they did penalize. The other master holds they did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more way to explain the two ברייתות. They speak about the same case, a שוגג, but disagree about whether to penalize him anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the two ברייתות really do argue. The one that forbids bringing the hand back holds קנסו שוגג אטו מזיד: we penalize even a mistake, so that people will not come to do it on purpose. The one that permits it holds that we do not penalize a שוגג because of a מזיד.

keyTerms.meaning: This one and that one (both cases)
They penalized a mistaken person because of a deliberate one
They disagree

steps.whatToRemember: So far, the two ברייתות about bringing the hand back have been explained in several ways: below versus above ten טפחים, before שבת versus after dark (which answers רב ביבי בר אביי's question: no permission), שוגג versus מזיד, or an argument over קנסו שוגג אטו מזיד. The next step begins one more explanation, based on where the object is brought back to.
steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of קנסו שוגג אטו מזיד, penalizing even a mistake to prevent deliberate wrongdoing, comes up many times across ש״ס.

phrases.english: And if you want, say: both this one and that one are about a mistake,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָכָא בְּקָנְסוּ שׁוֹגֵג אַטּוּ מֵזִיד קָמִיפַּלְגִי:
phrases.english: and here they disagree about whether they penalized a mistaken person because of a deliberate one:

phrases.aramaic: מָר סָבַר קָנְסוּ שׁוֹגֵג אַטּוּ מֵזִיד.
phrases.english: One master holds they penalized a mistaken person because of a deliberate one.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא that forbids bringing the hand back.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר לֹא קָנְסוּ שׁוֹגֵג אַטּוּ מֵזִיד.
phrases.english: And the other master holds they did not penalize a mistaken person because of a deliberate one.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא that permits bringing the hand back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another alternative to Step 11. It keeps both ברייתות in the same case (שוגג) and explains them as a real argument over a principle.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Real disagreement over a principle (קנסו שוגג אטו מזיד)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתות must speak about different cases, such as שוגג versus מזיד.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both are about a שוגג. They argue whether the חכמים penalize a שוגג because of a מזיד.

steps.title: Another answer: the difference is which courtyard he brings it back to
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives an alternative answer. The חכמים really do not penalize a שוגג, and the two ברייתות still do not contradict. The ברייתא that permits bringing the hand back is talking about bringing it back to the same חצר he is standing in.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say instead: really, the חכמים did not penalize a person who acted by mistake. And still there is no contradiction. Here, the ברייתא that allows it is talking about bringing it back to that same courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more way to settle the two ברייתות. It starts a new split: the permitting ברייתא is about bringing the object back into the same חצר where the person stands. The other half of this split continues on the next amud (4a).
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 12, one way to settle the ברייתות was that they argue whether a שוגג is penalized. Here the גמרא says everyone agrees there is no penalty for a שוגג. The difference between the ברייתות is instead the place he moves the object to. Bringing it back to his own חצר is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: introduces another possible answer
Really, in truth: keeps a position that was raised earlier
They (the חכמים) did not penalize
And it is not a difficulty: the sources do not truly contradict
To that same courtyard, the one he is standing in

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this answer has finished explaining both ברייתות. Here we only hear about the permitting ברייתא (same חצר). The forbidding ברייתא is explained at the start of the next amud (4a).
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer allows the ברייתות to fit together without saying the חכמים penalize a שוגג. It moves the difference from the person's state of mind to the place the object is going.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 12 explained the ברייתות as a מחלוקת about penalizing a שוגג. This step instead keeps the view that a שוגג is not penalized and splits the cases by location.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The contradiction would force us to say either that a שוגג is penalized or that the תנאים argue about it.
steps.terutzMaskana: No penalty for a שוגג. The permitting ברייתא is talking about returning the object to the same חצר. The forbidding ברייתא is explained by a different case on the next amud (4a).
